title: THE TRUTH WILL SET YOU FREE… BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN MISUNDERSTANDING WHAT JESUS MEANT ALL ALONG?
paragraphs: THE TRUTH WILL SET YOU FREE… BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN MISUNDERSTANDING WHAT JESUS MEANT ALL ALONG?

You can know the Bible, recognize the truth, defend your faith, and still be imprisoned by something you refuse to surrender. Jesus never promised freedom through information alone. What He revealed was far more personal, more confronting, and more beautiful than most people realize.
There is a kind of prison that doesn't have bars.
You can go to work inside it. Raise children inside it. Sing worship songs inside it. Post Bible verses on Facebook inside it.
You can even stand in church, lift your hands, whisper “Hallelujah,” and go home to the same invisible chains you've been dragging for years.
Nobody notices.
Because you've learned how to smile while you're struggling.
You've learned how to say “God is good” while secretly wondering why your heart still feels so heavy.
You've learned enough Scripture to encourage everyone else, yet there are nights when you cannot seem to believe those promises apply to you.
And perhaps the most painful part?
You know what's right. You know what's wrong. You know what the Bible says. But knowing hasn't always stopped you from returning to the very thing that's destroying your peace.
So when Jesus says, “The truth shall make you free,” something inside you wants to ask a question you might never say aloud.
Lord, if I know the truth… why am I still struggling?
That question deserves more than another inspirational quote.
It deserves an encounter with what Jesus actually said.
Because one of the most quoted promises in Christianity has also become one of the most misunderstood.
And when we return to its original setting, something extraordinary happens.
The words become more than a slogan.
They become a confrontation.
An invitation.
And for those willing to follow Jesus, a promise of freedom that reaches deeper than anything mere information could accomplish.
In John 8:32, Jesus declares:
“And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.” — John 8:32, KJV
Beautiful words.
But here is what we often overlook.
Jesus wasn't speaking to people who had never heard about God.
He was speaking to people who had religious knowledge, spiritual heritage, and confidence in what they believed.
And He was about to expose a slavery they didn't even recognize.
That should make every one of us pay attention.
Because sometimes the most dangerous prison is the one we've convinced ourselves doesn't exist.
To understand the promise, we have to read the sentence immediately before it.
Jesus says in John 8:31:
“If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed.” — KJV
Then comes the promise about knowing the truth.
Notice the order.
First, continuing in His word.
Then, knowing the truth.
Then, freedom.
Jesus does not present freedom as the automatic reward for collecting enough religious facts.
He connects it to remaining in His teaching as His disciples.
The original Greek makes this even more striking.
The phrase translated “If ye continue in my word” contains the verb μείνητε (meinēte), from μένω (menō), meaning to remain, abide, or continue.
It carries the idea of staying.
Not visiting Jesus when life falls apart.
Not borrowing His words when they support our preferences.
Not treating Scripture like an emergency exit while refusing to let Christ become Lord over our daily lives.
Remaining.
Staying with Him.
Continuing in what He has said.
Even when His words expose something we'd rather protect.
Even when obedience costs us comfort.
Even when the truth challenges the version of ourselves we've spent years defending.
And then Jesus says:
καὶ γνώσεσθε τὴν ἀλήθειαν, καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς.
Kai gnōsesthe tēn alētheian, kai hē alētheia eleutherōsei hymas.
“And you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” — John 8:32, translated from the Greek.
The word ἀλήθεια (alētheia) means truth.
The verb γνώσεσθε (gnōsesthe) means “you will know.”
And ἐλευθερώσει (eleutherōsei) means “will set free.”
These are not mysterious secret codes. Their significance comes from the sentence and the larger conversation.
Jesus is not condemning factual knowledge. Christianity is grounded in real truth about what God has done in history.
But in this passage, the freedom He promises is not simply intellectual enlightenment.
The very next verses reveal why.
When Jesus speaks of freedom, His listeners respond:
“We be Abraham's seed, and were never in bondage to any man.” — John 8:33, KJV.
Think about that response.
They appeal to their ancestry.
Their identity.
Their religious inheritance.
And they resist the implication that they need liberation.
Yet Jesus answers with words that strip away every comfortable illusion:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.” — John 8:34, KJV
There it is.
The prison Jesus is addressing.
Sin.
Not merely ignorance.
Not simply a lack of education.
Not an unfortunate shortage of motivational thinking.
Sin.
The power that makes human beings choose what wounds them, defend what corrupts them, and hide what desperately needs to be brought into the light.
And suddenly, this conversation is no longer about people standing in Jerusalem two thousand years ago.
It's about us.
It's about the husband who knows that harsh words can wound his wife, yet keeps allowing anger to rule his tongue.
It's about the woman who knows that bitterness is poisoning her heart, yet replays the same betrayal every night because forgiveness feels like surrendering justice.
It's about the believer who knows what Scripture teaches about purity, yet returns to a private habit that leaves them ashamed.
It's about the person who knows that lying is wrong but has built an entire public image around pretending.
It's about the churchgoer who knows the language of grace but cannot stop measuring other people by their worst mistakes.
And perhaps it's about someone reading this right now.
Someone who loves Jesus.
Someone who genuinely wants to change.
Someone who has promised God, more than once, that this would be the last time.
But the struggle returned.
And with it came the whisper:
Maybe I'm not really His.
Listen carefully.
The presence of a struggle does not automatically mean your faith is counterfeit.
But neither should we mistake the desire to change for the act of repentance.
Jesus calls us beyond hiding, beyond excuses, and beyond surrendering to sin as though it owns us.
And the good news is that He does not merely stand outside our prison telling us to try harder.
He came to accomplish the freedom we could never purchase through our own righteousness.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because John 8 doesn't end with Jesus exposing slavery.
In verse 36, He declares:
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.” — John 8:36, KJV
Read that again.
Not “If you become intelligent enough.”
Not “If you memorize enough verses.”
Not “If you successfully conceal every failure.”
Not even “If you manage to repair yourself.”
If the Son makes you free.
The freedom is His to give.
And the One offering it is not merely another religious teacher.
He is the Son.
The very One who says in John 14:6:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” — KJV
Do you see the connection?
The truth Jesus teaches is inseparable from who He is.
He is not saying that facts don't matter.
He is revealing that the saving truth of God finds its fullest expression in Him.
Truth has a face.
Truth entered our broken world.
Truth walked among sinners.
Truth confronted hypocrisy without becoming hypocritical.
Truth touched the unclean.
Truth welcomed the repentant.
Truth stood before human injustice, was condemned, and went to the cross.
And the One who is Truth rose again.
That changes everything.
Because the deepest answer to our bondage is not merely learning another religious principle.
It is being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Picture a man sitting alone in his car outside a church.
The service has ended.
Families are driving home.
The parking lot is almost empty.
But he cannot bring himself to turn the key.
He heard the sermon.
He sang the songs.
He greeted people who asked how he was doing.
“I'm blessed,” he told them.
And perhaps he meant it.
But his phone is beside him.
And on that phone are conversations he knows he should never have started.
There are messages he has hidden.
Choices he has rationalized.
Promises he has broken.
He remembers his wife trusting him.
He remembers the man he once wanted to become.
And now he is staring through the windshield, wondering how someone who knows so much about God could have wandered so far from obedience.
He doesn't need another excuse.
He doesn't need someone to tell him that his choices don't matter.
He needs the truth.
But he is terrified of what telling the truth will cost him.
Perhaps that is where you are.
Not necessarily in a parked car.
Maybe in your bedroom.
Maybe at work.
Maybe sitting beside someone who has no idea how much you're hurting.
Maybe carrying a secret that has become heavier every year.
And this is where the enemy's deception becomes especially cruel.
Sin tempts us with the promise of freedom.
Do what you want.
You deserve this.
Nobody has to know.
You can stop whenever you choose.
Then, after we fall, shame begins making its own demands.
Hide.
Pretend.
Don't tell anyone.
God must be tired of you.
The very thing that promised freedom becomes a source of captivity.
But Jesus tells the truth about sin precisely because He came to save sinners.
His confrontation is not an invitation to despair.
It is a call to repentance.
And repentance is not merely feeling terrible about what we've done.
The New Testament word μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance—a change of mind and direction involving a genuine turning from sin toward God.
It is not a magical word that erases consequences.
It is not a performance designed to earn forgiveness.
It is a response to God's grace, involving honest acknowledgment of sin and a turning toward the Savior.
There may be apologies to make.
Relationships to repair.
Secrets to confess appropriately.
Temptations to flee.
Boundaries to establish.
Trusted spiritual leaders or counselors to approach.
And some consequences may remain even after genuine forgiveness.
But none of those realities cancel the mercy available in Christ.
First John 1:9 tells us:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because the sacrifice of Jesus is sufficient.
At the cross, God's holiness and mercy are not competing stories.
Christ bears sin, and through Him forgiveness is offered.
Romans 5:8 declares that God demonstrated His love toward us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we successfully repaired our reputations.
Not after we made ourselves worthy.
While we were still sinners.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain in rebellion.
Not a religious excuse to continue harming people.
Grace saves, forgives, and teaches us to turn away from ungodliness, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
Grace doesn't make holiness unnecessary.
Grace makes a new life possible.
And perhaps that is what you need to hear today.
You are not beyond the reach of Jesus because your story has ugly chapters.
You are not required to pretend those chapters were beautiful.
You are not asked to rename darkness as light.
You are invited to bring the truth into the presence of the One who saves.
Look at Peter.
He knew Jesus personally.
He had witnessed miracles.
He had heard teachings that transformed lives.
He even declared that he was ready to die with his Lord.
Yet when fear pressed against him, he denied knowing Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61–62 records that Jesus turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine that moment.
The terrible realization.
The memory of his promises.
The sound of his own denial still echoing.
The unbearable knowledge that he had failed the One he loved.
Peter didn't need more information about whether denying Jesus was wrong.
He already knew.
He needed mercy.
He needed restoration.
And after the resurrection, Jesus met him again.
In John 21, the risen Christ questioned Peter about his love and entrusted him with caring for His sheep.
Jesus did not pretend the denial never happened.
But Peter's failure did not become the final word over his life.
That is not cheap grace.
That is resurrection grace.
The kind that confronts the truth and still opens a future.
The kind that refuses to let sin have the last word over someone who turns back to Christ.
The kind that transforms a broken disciple into a witness of the risen Lord.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by changing the historical facts.
Peter really denied Him.
The tears were real.
The failure was real.
But so was the resurrection.
So was the restoration.
And so was the calling that followed.
This matters because sometimes we think freedom means never remembering what happened.
Sometimes we imagine that being forgiven means never feeling grief over what we did.
Sometimes we assume that if Jesus has truly changed us, every temptation, emotional wound, and painful consequence must disappear immediately.
But Scripture gives us a more substantial hope.
Romans 6 teaches that believers united with Christ are no longer to live as slaves to sin.
That doesn't mean Christians become incapable of temptation or failure.
It means sin is no longer their rightful master.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
That promise belongs to those who are in Christ.
It is not a declaration that sin is harmless.
It is the glorious announcement that those who belong to Jesus are no longer under sin's condemning verdict.
And sanctification—the lifelong work of growing in holiness—continues as we walk by the Spirit.
There may still be battles.
There may still be tears.
There may be days when obedience feels costly.
But freedom in Christ is deeper than the absence of difficulty.
It means you no longer have to call darkness your home.
You can confess instead of conceal.
You can repent instead of rationalize.
You can seek help instead of pretending to be invincible.
You can forgive without claiming that injustice was acceptable.
You can tell the truth even when lies once seemed safer.
You can obey Christ because His grace is at work in you.
And when you stumble, you can return to Him rather than running farther into the darkness.
Not because you are strong enough to save yourself.
But because Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Now return to the words that began this entire conversation.
“You shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”
What if we've been quoting that verse while overlooking the very next confrontation?
What if we've celebrated the language of freedom while resisting the Lordship of the One who gives it?
What if we have spent years asking God to remove the consequences of our choices while refusing to surrender the choices themselves?
These questions are uncomfortable.
They should be.
But they are not meant to push you away from Christ.
They are meant to bring you nearer.
Because the truth that exposes our sin also points us toward the Savior.
And this is where we must make a distinction.
There is a difference between being informed about Jesus and trusting Jesus.
A person can study the historical evidence for Christianity and still reject Christ.
A person can explain the doctrine of grace and still refuse to repent.
A person can quote verses about forgiveness while withholding mercy from others.
Even the religious leaders in John 8 were familiar with Scripture and confident in their spiritual heritage.
Yet Jesus challenged them to recognize their need for Him.
Knowledge matters deeply.
Sound doctrine matters.
Understanding Scripture in context matters.
But biblical knowledge is meant to lead us into faithful trust, worship, obedience, and love.
It was never meant to become a hiding place for spiritual pride.
Jesus says in John 8:31 that His true disciples continue in His word.
Not merely admire it.
Continue in it.
And that means the truth we claim to believe must eventually confront the life we actually live.
Perhaps you have been reading this with a particular name in mind.
Someone who hurt you.
Someone who betrayed you.
Someone whose choices caused wounds you still carry.
Or perhaps the name is your own.
Maybe you are remembering a version of yourself that you desperately wish you could erase.
An affair.
An addiction.
A lie.
An abortion.
A betrayal.
A season of unbelief.
A relationship you damaged.
A child you neglected.
A moment when you chose fear over faithfulness.
Whatever the story, please hear this carefully.
Your sin must not be minimized.
The people you hurt must not be forgotten.
Repentance does not eliminate the need for accountability or restitution where appropriate.
But the Gospel declares that no repentant sinner must remain defined forever by the worst thing they have done.
Christ offers forgiveness and a new identity to those who come to Him in faith.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — KJV
That does not mean your memories instantly disappear.
It means that in Christ, a new creation has begun.
Your past may explain part of your story.
It does not have to rule your future.
Your failure may have consequences.
It does not have to become your master.
Your shame may be loud.
It is not greater than the Gospel.
And the Savior who called Peter back from bitter tears still calls sinners to repentance and faith today.
Maybe this is the moment to stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
Maybe this is the moment to stop calling a secret sin a private weakness when you know it is becoming a master.
Maybe this is the moment to tell God the truth you've been afraid to say aloud.

Lord, I know the verses. I know the right answers. But there are places in my life where I have resisted You. I need more than information. I need Your mercy. I need Your power to change. Teach me to remain in Your word. Lead me into genuine repentance. Forgive me through Jesus Christ. Help me walk in the freedom You have purchased.
There is no magic in the wording of that prayer.
The hope is not in the eloquence of your confession.
The hope is in Jesus Christ—crucified, risen, and able to save.
And if you're reading this while feeling completely exhausted from fighting the same battle, please don't confuse the call to repentance with a demand to heal alone.
Reach out to a trustworthy pastor, mature believer, or qualified counselor where needed.
Bring what is hidden into appropriate, safe accountability.
Open the Scriptures again.
Pray even when your words are trembling.
Take the next obedient step.
And keep looking to Christ.
Not to your own perfection as the foundation of your salvation.
To Christ.
Because freedom begins with His saving work, and a life of discipleship learns to walk in what His grace has made possible.
I wonder how many people on your Facebook friends list are quietly fighting battles like these.
The father who provides for everyone but privately feels he has failed his family.
The young woman who smiles in photographs but cries when nobody is watching.
The teenager who has started believing that one terrible mistake has ruined their future.
The believer who has stopped praying because shame keeps whispering that God doesn't want to hear their voice.
The person who has never understood Christianity beyond rules and religious traditions.
And the friend who thinks Jesus came only to condemn people like them.
Perhaps they have heard the phrase “The truth will set you free” a thousand times.
But perhaps nobody has ever shown them the Savior at the center of that promise.
That's why sharing biblical truth matters.
Not because a Facebook post can save a soul.
Only Jesus saves.
But God can use His Word, faithfully communicated by ordinary people, to awaken questions, encourage repentance, strengthen believers, and point hurting hearts toward Christ.
Not as a performance of faith.
Not to prove that you're more spiritual than anyone else.
But because someone who follows you may need to encounter these Scriptures today.
And if a particular person is struggling privately, consider sending it to them personally with gentleness rather than exposing their pain publicly.
Sometimes one thoughtful message can begin a conversation that someone has been afraid to start.
And I want to invite you to do something else.
Not for appearances.
Not because you owe strangers the details of your wounds.
But because there is something powerful about refusing to let shame convince you that you are the only one still learning to surrender.
You do not have to disclose a private sin or painful experience publicly.
And if God has brought you through a season of repentance and restoration, consider sharing a brief testimony of His grace.
Someone reading your words may discover that they are not alone in their struggle—and that hope is still possible in Jesus Christ.
And invite your family, friends, fellow believers, those who have drifted from church, and even those who are still questioning Christianity to follow along.
The Gospel is too precious to keep locked inside our comfortable circles.
There is also something important I want to share about the mission behind Gospel Warrior.
Every article, devotional, and biblical resource we create is part of a larger desire: to help people encounter the truth of Scripture and grow in their understanding of Jesus Christ.
We want that library to keep growing.
We want more people to have access to resources that help them study Scripture, strengthen their faith, and understand the Gospel.
And that kind of work takes time, effort, resources, and the faithful support of people who believe in the mission.
It cannot purchase forgiveness, blessing, or spiritual standing.
Those things are not for sale.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by financial contributions.
The greater purpose remains discipleship.
Helping people open their Bibles.
Helping struggling believers return to Christ.
Helping families encounter biblical truth.
Helping people understand that the Gospel is not about pretending to be righteous, but about coming to the righteous Savior who redeems sinners.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
And faithfully living out the Gospel in your own home, workplace, church, and community is an extraordinary way to glorify God.
It is about pointing people to Jesus.
The same Jesus who looked at religious people who thought they were already free and told them the truth about their bondage.
The same Jesus who refused to flatter sinners but willingly died to save them.
The same Jesus who restored Peter.
The same Jesus who declared that if the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.
And that brings us back to the question we began with.
Is “The truth will set you free” about knowing facts?
Yes, truth involves what is real, and knowing the truth of God's revelation matters.
But in John 8, Jesus is speaking about something far deeper than acquiring information.
He is calling people to continue in His word, become His genuine disciples, recognize their slavery to sin, and receive the freedom only the Son can give.
The truth is not an impersonal technique for improving your life.
It is God's revelation leading us to Jesus Christ.
And Jesus is not merely interested in making you better informed.
He came to redeem you.
So the next time you hear someone quote John 8:32, remember John 8:36.
Remember the Son.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember Peter's tears and his restoration.
Remember that grace never requires you to lie about your sin.
It invites you to confess it and turn toward the Savior.
And tonight, when the noise quiets down and you're alone with the thoughts you've been avoiding, perhaps you will remember this:
You can spend your entire life learning how to describe the prison—or you can come to the Son who alone can set you free.
The door to salvation is not opened by your ability to impress God.
It is opened through the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Remain in His Word.
Walk in His truth.
And when your past tries to convince you that nothing can ever change, remember that the risen Christ is still in the business of redeeming lives.
The chains you learned to live with were never meant to become the name you answer to—Jesus calls you to belong to Him.
